title: How Consumed by Social Comparison Are You
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article draws a line between healthy benchmarking and destructive fixation on how one measures up to others. In small doses, comparison motivates improvement and offers role models; taken too far, it breeds envy, anxiety, perfectionism, and poor decision-making driven by keeping up rather than doing what's right. The piece singles out social media as an amplifier, since curated images of others' success distort people's sense of their own standing. Its prescription is to judge success against one's own goals and focus attention on learning and progress rather than on others' achievements.
points: Comparison in small doses can motivate improvement and provide useful role models
Excessive comparison fuels anxiety, envy, perfectionism, and poor decision-making
Social media amplifies comparison by showcasing idealized, unrepresentative images of others' success
The antidote is judging progress against your own goals rather than against other people's outcomes
quotes: In small doses, social comparison allows people to benchmark their skills and talents against others to get better.
Excessive social comparison, whether it springs from jealousy or a need to be viewed as more successful than others, produces feelings of inadequacy and anxiety
Research proves that the idealized images of others’ lives and successes promoted on social media heighten personal dissatisfaction and emotional distress.
Smart people come to the realization that the comparison game is unwinnable—there is always someone more skilled, more accomplished, and more polished.
The best leaders keep their eyes down and attend to their own advancement.
